title: Super-for-housing push ignites fight over affordability risks
full_text:
Shadow housing and homelessness minister Andrew Bragg has called for Australia’s retirement system to prioritise outright home ownership, arguing workers should be able to use their superannuation savings to purchase a first home during a media briefing at the Australian Computer Society in Sydney on Wednesday.
Drawing on the latest Intergenerational Report (IGR), Bragg said housing remained integral to the three pillars of Australia’s retirement system: private savings, superannuation and the Age Pension.
“The IGR says that the housing status is a strong predictor of the success of your retirement, and so none of this will be surprising to you because the economic and psychological benefits of home ownership transcend any other financial interest that you may be able to have,” Bragg said.
“There is nothing wrong with choosing to rent to make that very clear, but we don’t want to make renting in retirement compulsory.”
Bragg said the proportion of retirees renting had risen from 6 per cent two decades ago to 12 per cent, with projections indicating the number could approach 1 million over the coming decade.
“I want to stop those people from being retired renters, unless they choose to be that way,” he said. “I don’t want this to become a compulsory design feature of a retirement policy which doesn’t work together. I want the housing policy to work in concert with superannuation, with social security, so that we can look at all these things together.”
The Coalition took a policy to the 2022 and 2025 elections that would have allowed Australians to withdraw up to $50,000 from their super to buy their first home. Bragg pointed to mandatory savings systems in Singapore, Canada and New Zealand that allow savings to be used towards housing.
However, the Super Members Council (SMC) rejected the proposal, warning early access to super could lift house prices and rents, reduce retirement savings and ultimately increase reliance on the Age Pension.
The SMC cited New Zealand as evidence that such a policy could worsen affordability, claiming house prices there grew at twice Australia’s rate up to the 2022 market peak after a comparable scheme was introduced.
Over the same period, home ownership among New Zealanders in their 30s fell by 7 percentage points, according to the council.
Research commissioned by the SMC in 2025 also found allowing first home buyers to withdraw super for a deposit could lift Australian house prices by up to 10.3 per cent.
“As respected economists have consistently noted, the key to improve housing affordability is to boost housing supply – not to tell people to withdraw their super early which would just push up house prices,” SMC chief executive Misha Schubert said.
“These sorts of policy ideas would just make cost of living pressures worse – not better – for battling Australians.”
Bragg disputed the argument that super withdrawals would necessarily inflate house prices, contrasting opposition to the Coalition’s policy with the government’s 5 per cent deposit scheme.
“So, while I will not concede that the last policy will necessarily do that, I would argue the case that an unrestricted free government scheme could do that and has done that,” he said.
Bragg also questioned the separation of super and housing policy, pointing to data showing 32 per cent of super lump sums had been used to repay mortgages during the previous year.
“Effectively, we now run a system. We give people an enormous amount of tax concessions to save in superannuation, then they take the money out and pay off a mortgage at the end of their mandatory savings period,” he said.
“Now, surely that is a very rigid and technocratic approach that we should look at.”
Under Bragg’s proposed hierarchy for retirement policy, owning a home outright would take precedence, followed by accumulating income-producing assets capable of supplementing or replacing the Age Pension.
“The first priority is owning a residence outright in retirement is the priority of the retirement policy in Australia that must be the priority,” he said.
“The secondary priority is only assets which can help give you an income, which can either supplement or replace reliance on the age pension.”
While Bragg positioned the proposal as an addition to compulsory super rather than an attempt to dismantle it, the SMC warned weakening preservation rules could undermine projected reductions in Age Pension expenditure.
The IGR projected Age Pension spending would fall from 2.3 per cent of gross domestic product to 1.8 per cent by 2066, while the proportion of people above pension age relying on government income support was expected to decline from 66 per cent to 52 per cent.
The SMC compared Australia’s projected pension burden with an estimated 10 per cent of GDP in the United Kingdom, 8 per cent in Canada, 7 per cent in New Zealand and 6 per cent in the United States.
“Cashing out super would push up Age Pension costs for taxpayers, leaving less money to fund the services that battling households rely on – hospitals, medicines, schools, roads, and drought and flood relief,” Schubert said.
Research cited by the council found 80 per cent of Australians believed super would be critical to their retirement living standards, while 88 per cent of older Australians were concerned about policies expanding early access.
More than 70 per cent of seniors surveyed by National Seniors Australia said they would not have accumulated enough retirement savings without compulsory super.
Bragg argued Australia nevertheless needed to reconsider a system that could leave workers with substantial super balances but no home of their own, potentially forcing them to rent from institutional investors during retirement.
“You may have a situation where that individual, that average worker, may end up renting in retirement from a super fund rather than living in a house of their own,” he said.
“We want to add to this debate, not subtract from it. We want home ownership to be a clear objective. We need to objectively look at the data. We should call out incoherence and idiocy, and the world has changed since super started in ’92.”
